items.title: What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture
items.summary:
Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above .

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade…
items.t: What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture

items.title: The Amazing Inventions of Ancient Greece: From Plato’s Alarm Clock to Ancient Flamethrowers
items.summary:
“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time , a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the Diolkos , recently mentioned…
items.t: The Amazing Inventions of Ancient Greece: From Plato’s Alarm Clock to Ancient Flamethrowers

items.title: The Psychedelic Animated Video for Kraftwerk’s “Autobahn” (1979)
items.summary:
Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band members still looked like well-meaning, bookish hippies, 1974’s “Autobahn” is considered Year Zero for the denizens of the Electric Café, the four German robots who made human music with machines.

This cel-drawn animation by Roger Mainwood was made in 1979 to promote “Autobahn,” after most of the culture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bopping around pop culture again. By that last year of the ’70s, Omni magazine was a year old, music was sifting through the shockwaves left by Bowie’s Low and Heroes , analog was flirting with digital, and the world was ready to drive on that long, electric highway.

Mainwood’s protagonist is part alien, part human, and he begins looking around in awe in his hip goggles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muybridge loop, only to wind up floating, flying, sailing and swimming through a landscape indebted to Peter Max, Push Pin Studios, underground comix, and 1930s modernism.

Mainwood had just graduated from London’s Royal College of Art Film and Television School, and was commissioned by John Halas, the Hungarian immigrant who became known as the Father of British Animation, for Kraftwerk’s record label. The label wanted to put out one of the first music Laserdiscs. (Halas, by the way, directed a very UPA-influenced short called “Automania” in 1963 ). According to Mainwood, he still doesn’t know if the band liked the short or even…
items.t: The Psychedelic Animated Video for Kraftwerk’s “Autobahn” (1979)

items.title: The Directing Genius of Akira Kurosawa Explained
items.summary:
Generations of Westerners have come to appreciate Japanese cinema through the films of Akira Kurosawa , but many have been shocked to find out that Kurosawa himself isn’t as beloved in Japan as they’d imagined. It’s less that his homeland rejects him than that his work has been regarded there as a somewhat foreign taste. That judgment must have something to it: despite their thoroughly Japanese settings, Throne of Blood , The Bad Sleep Well , and Ran were, after all, Shakespeare adaptations, and Kurosawa spoke openly of structuring his stories in the manner of not just traditional Japanese theater, but also symphonies. Consider, too, the way his films continue to inspire Western remakes, from The Magnificent Seven and A Fistful of Dollars in the nineteen-sixties to Living and Highest 2 Lowest in this decade.

Nor can it be a coincidence that the appreciative voices opening the StudioBinder video on Kurosawa’s genius above belong to Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, and George Lucas. Yet this most internationally celebrated of all Japanese filmmakers can’t, ultimately, have been just a Westerner in disguise, since his work gives viewers around the world something that their domestic movies don’t.

Whatever the extent to which he hybridized the cinematic sensibilities of Japan and Hollywood, he did so through his uncompromising personal involvement in every stage of the process. “The role of the director encompasses the coaching of the actors, the cinematography, the sound recording, the art direction, the music, the editing, and the dubbing and sound mixing,” he once said,…
items.t: The Directing Genius of Akira Kurosawa Explained

items.title: Explore 250,000 Articles from Salon’s 31-Year History at the Internet Archive
items.summary:
Earlier this month, Salon announced that it’s ceasing publication after 31 years. In its farewell address, the magazine writes: “The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable.” We can sympathize.

Over the 20 years we have served you, we have watched quality websites come and go. Some once-vibrant sites have gone entirely dark. Today, if you want to sift through the remains of the early internet, you can head over to the Internet Archive —a site that “captures and stores over one trillion web pages to safeguard digital history and prevent the rewriting or erasure of online records.” In the case of Salon , the Internet Archive has launched Salon Explorer , a “new interface for discovering Salon’s archived journalism.” According to a new blog post from the Internet Archive, the tool lets you browse more than 250,000 articles and explore the work of over 20,000 writers, with filters that make it easier to find stories you may have missed. If it isn’t your preferred interface, you can also browse Salon.com using the Wayback Machine . RIP Salon, long live the Internet Archive.

Enter the Salon Explorer here .
